claims.text: An integrated ab initio molecular-dynamics and machine-learning interatomic-potential framework can explicitly model electron-phonon coupling in disordered HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework will independently predict and separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework will reduce predictive error by approximately 20% relative to Debye-temperature-based or DFT-elastic-property models.
A minimally impure HfNbTaTiZr sample approximates the defect-free state relevant to low-temperature studies.
Adding 1 wt.% oxygen provides a representative high-temperature, non-ideal HfNbTaTiZr condition.
An interatomic-potential molecular-dynamics framework can account for local chemical disorder.
The proposed framework can account specifically for minor oxygen impurities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Multi-element disorder and oxygen impurities produce local variations in atomic mass and force constants in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit simulation of electron-phonon interactions in a disordered lattice decouples phonon and electronic heat-transport channels.
Separating the two transport channels will produce conductivity components that better represent actual thermal transport.
Earlier averaged-property models inherently conflate lattice and electronic heat transport.
For oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr between 300 and 1200 K, the predicted total thermal conductivity will be 10–17 W/(K·m).
Existing Debye- and DFT-elastic-property-based conductivity approaches use defect-free bulk crystals.
Existing Debye- and DFT-based approaches do not isolate lattice and electronic conductivity contributions and have larger prediction errors.
The claimed improvement applies from cryogenic temperatures below 200 K through 1200 K and near an oxygen level of 1 wt.%.
Accurate parameterization of electron-phonon interactions is challenging in the presence of atomic-scale disorder and impurities.
Inelastic neutron scattering can independently determine the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution for the proposed comparison.
Hall and electrical-conductivity measurements combined with the Wiedemann-Franz law can independently determine electronic thermal conductivity across the proposed temperature range.
Failure to achieve an approximately 20% error reduction or failure of either separated component to agree within experimental uncertainty would falsify the hypothesis.
